# The Peculiar Gift of Boredom

I want to talk about boredom, that strange state we spend so much energy trying to escape. Not the clinical kind of boredom that gets pathologized in medical literature, but the ordinary, everyday boredom that most of us experience regularly and yet rarely examine closely. We treat it like a malfunction, a sign that something has gone wrong with our entertainment system or our productivity machine. But I think boredom might be one of the more valuable experiences we can have, particularly in a world increasingly designed to eliminate it.

There's a peculiar contradiction in modern life. We have access to more forms of entertainment, information, and stimulation than any humans in history. I can open my phone and within seconds access thousands of hours of video, millions of articles, countless games, social feeds updating in real time. And yet, paradoxically, we seem to experience boredom more acutely than ever. People describe themselves as "bored" while scrolling through infinite content. The stimulation has become so constant, so readily available, that nothing quite satisfies anymore. We've created a kind of hedonic treadmill powered by algorithms.

I think part of what's happening is that we've confused boredom with emptiness. Boredom used to mean something specific: a situation where external stimulation was limited, where you had to sit with your own mind. Now, we use the word to describe a kind of frenetic dissatisfaction, the feeling that what we're currently consuming isn't engaging enough, that we should be doing something more stimulating. We swipe left, we change the channel, we refresh our feeds. The anxiety of potential boredom drives us to constantly seek novelty.

What I'm interested in is what happens when you actually let yourself be bored. Not deliberately torturing yourself, but allowing situations to unfold where boredom becomes unavoidable, and then observing what occurs in that space.

When I was a child, summer days were long and surprisingly boring. There were periods where there was genuinely nothing to do. No devices to check, no streaming services, limited television. My friends were inside or away. I found myself alone in my backyard or my room with very little external stimulation. And in that boredom, something remarkable would happen. My mind would begin generating its own content. I'd play elaborate imaginative games, create stories, rearrange my room, experiment with things, draw, think about problems that interested me. The boredom was the condition that forced my creativity to activate.

I notice this doesn't happen when I'm constantly stimulated. If I have my phone available, if there's always something new to engage with, that generative space simply doesn't open. My mind stays in consumption mode, reactive rather than creative. The external stimulation crowds out the internal voice that might have something to offer.

There's research suggesting this is real. Studies on mind-wandering and the default mode network of the brain show that when we're not focused on external tasks, our minds do something different—they make connections, integrate memories, explore possibilities. This default mode isn't a bug; it seems to be crucial for creativity, problem-solving, and psychological integration. Yet we've become increasingly hostile to the conditions that allow it. We treat idle time as wasted time. We optimize every moment for productivity or entertainment.

I wonder if what we call boredom is sometimes actually the sound of our internal systems trying to activate. It's an uncomfortable feeling because we've lost the tolerance for it. A mild version of that feeling—what I'd call understimulation—is necessary for that generative mode to engage. But instead of allowing ourselves to experience it, we immediately reach for our phones, turn on music, start planning something. We've made understimulation something to be avoided at all costs.

There's also something valuable about boredom in terms of perspective and values. When you're perpetually entertained, when you're always consuming content chosen by algorithms optimized to engage you, it's easy to lose touch with what actually matters to you. Entertainment is someone else's art, someone else's vision. Boredom creates space to notice your own desires, your own curiosities. It's quieter, less seductive than well-crafted entertainment, but it's more authentic to who you actually are.

I've noticed this with reading. I used to read books I didn't particularly like because I'd made a commitment to them, and I'd have to sit with them through moments of boredom. Now I have hundreds of entertainment options at hand, and the moment a book stops perfectly engaging me, I can switch to something else. This seems like freedom, and in some sense it is. But I think I also miss something from the experience of pushing through boredom in a book, of having to engage more deeply with something that doesn't immediately appeal. Sometimes that leads to unexpected appreciation. And the act of staying with something despite its difficulty, despite moments of disengagement, is itself valuable. It's a kind of discipline that affects how you approach other challenges.

There's also a social dimension to this. Boredom used to be something you experienced communally sometimes. You'd be stuck somewhere with other people, with limited options, and out of that boredom, conversation would emerge. Real, unscripted conversation. Not the curated versions we share online. I think about how much differently my extended family gatherings work now. Before, when there were limits on entertainment, people would actually sit and talk. Now everyone is checking their phones, escaping into individual content streams. The boredom that used to be a driver of connection has been eliminated.

I also want to acknowledge that boredom can be unpleasant. I'm not arguing that it's some pure good. Acute boredom, especially without hope of it ending, can be genuinely distressing. The boredom of a long car ride with nothing to do, no one to talk to, and no end in sight. The boredom of a boring job where you're trapped for eight hours. This kind of boredom can be alienating and painful. But I think the answer isn't to become incapable of experiencing any boredom—it's to preserve some capacity for it while recognizing situations where it's genuinely harmful.

What I'm suggesting is a more nuanced relationship with boredom than the current approach of total elimination. The goal shouldn't be to never be bored. The goal might be to be selectively bored, to preserve time and space where boredom is possible, while also having resources to escape it when it becomes genuinely harmful.

I think of boredom tolerance as a kind of resilience. If you've never experienced boredom, or only the mildest version of it, then any situation without perfect stimulation becomes unbearable. You become dependent on external entertainment for basic contentment. But if you develop tolerance for boredom, you become more resilient. You can manage situations that aren't perfectly optimized for engagement. You can be alone with your thoughts without it being torture. You can sit with difficulty.

There's also something I'd call the paradox of interesting boredom. Some of the most interesting moments of my life have come from periods of what I'd initially experience as boredom. A quiet morning with no plans, where I'm not engaging with anything external—in those spaces, thoughts surface that wouldn't otherwise. Insights emerge. Decisions become clearer. Creativity activates. The boredom is the price of entry to those spaces.

I think about how artists and writers often talk about the importance of boredom. They describe it as essential to their process. They need time that isn't stimulated, isn't "productive," to let their creative work germinate. They're not talking about entertainment boredom—the frustration of not having enough diversions. They're talking about the fertile boredom that opens creative possibility.

One of the things I've become aware of is how the war on boredom has commercialized it. Every moment of potential boredom is now a market opportunity. Bored on the toilet? Here's a game. Bored waiting in line? Here's social media. Bored before sleep? Here's a podcast. Every gap in stimulation is something to be filled with a product or service. This is profitable for the companies creating the entertainment, but I wonder what we lose in the process.

I wonder if part of the alienation and dissatisfaction so many people report might actually be connected to this inability to tolerate any boredom. If your internal rewards system has been trained by algorithms designed to hit dopamine targets, then ordinary life will seem less engaging. A conversation with a friend might seem boring compared to a perfectly edited entertainment product. Ordinary meals might seem less stimulating than a engineered snack. This seems like a recipe for perpetual dissatisfaction.

I'm not arguing for a return to some pre-digital past. Those earlier eras had their own problems, their own ways of being unsatisfying. But I think there's something worth preserving from that experience of boredom, something valuable about space that isn't optimized for engagement.

What would it look like to reclaim some tolerance for boredom? I think it might mean periodically choosing not to fill available time with stimulation. Taking walks without podcasts. Eating meals without devices. Sitting quietly without the radio. Not all the time—the modern world does offer genuine goods that entertainment provides. But regularly, deliberately, creating space where boredom becomes possible.

It might also mean being more intentional about what we do choose to engage with. Instead of consuming whatever algorithm presents next, actually selecting things we think are worth our attention. Finishing books we find challenging. Having conversations without the safety net of our phones. These aren't particularly novel suggestions, but they take on new meaning in the context of an environment actively hostile to boredom.

What strikes me about boredom is that it's honest. Entertainment lies to you—not maliciously, but by design. It's engineered to be more engaging than reality. It's a best-case version of stimulation. Boredom, by contrast, is just life as it actually is for many stretches—not terrible, but not dramatically engaging either. Learning to tolerate and even appreciate that might be one of the more mature adjustments we can make.

I think we need boredom. Not as a failure state to be corrected, but as a necessary part of being human. The capacity to be alone with your thoughts, to sit with understimulation, to let your mind wander where it will—these seem essential to developing as thoughtful, creative people. The alternative is perpetual reactivity, always responding to the next stimulus, never generating anything from within.

The irony is that boredom is free, and the alternatives are often quite expensive. The entertainment industry spends billions to create the most engaging possible content, to make boredom impossible to tolerate. Meanwhile, boredom just happens. It doesn't require monetization or infrastructure. It's just what's left when you're not being entertained.

So I'm interested in boredom not as a problem to solve, but as a resource we've been throwing away. A weird kind of gift hidden in something we've been trained to find unpleasant. The space where your own mind gets to speak, where you're not being sold anything, where creativity can germinate and genuine thoughts can emerge.

The challenge is to preserve some relationship with it, even in a world increasingly designed to make it impossible.
